title: Debbie Bennett's research: Papa Laine and ragtime to jazz
summary: Wiggs names Papa Laine as the first documented bandleader and says early music was ragtime; Allen says history has conflicting accounts.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Oh, this is Debbie Bennett. And I'm doing a research paper on the origin of jazz. And I've heard so many different stories about it, I don't know which one to believe. I've heard that the Negroes had brought about jazz. And I heard a gentleman on the air a little while before me about a Tom Brown. And I was wondering if I'm...
You want to know what's the right scoop?
Okay, let's turn to Mr. Johnny Wiggs.

Well, the first man that they have any history, documented history on, of course, there was jazz before him. But the first one that they have documented, as I say, is Papa Lane. He had bands in the parades, which were very numerous around New Orleans in the early days. And he had maybe five or six bands, which he supplied for various occasions. And one of the main occasions in those days was picnics. And he supplied bands for the picnics and for the parades. And he played a sort of a ragtime, which gradually, I imagine, changed over to what we consider jazz now. What would you think, Dick? You better help me out on this, Dick. Dick is a historian, you know.

My feeling is that I've interviewed a lot of these people. I'm fortunate enough to interview Papa Lane several times. But you go to books, you go to all these different sources, and you always seem to be at least one step away. You talk to Papa Lane, and he tells you about his older brothers. Well, what do we know about Buddy Bolden, who came before him? And it's just you never can quite get to the exact truth. What the historians say is that history is a tattered cloak. And there are many different opinions. If she wants to do research, she's going to find that it's true in any field, that there are going to be conflicting stories. And you have to, if you're going to write a paper on it.

Yeah. Well, I heard most of the Negro bands were considered marching bands. Like, I heard that Papa Lane was a marching band, and not a jazz band, it's so-called. And I was wondering, do you have any information on this? Well, he was, his band was made up of people that played by ear. Now, ear music usually comes out what we call jazz, or ragtime. In the early days, it was ragtime-ish, and it has changed, and it has become more fluid in recent times. It's beginning, as far as I'm concerned, when I heard Joe Oliver and then Louis Armstrong and Bix Beiderback. It's much more fluid. And also, Jelly Roll Martin, don't let's forget him. Jelly Roll Martin has the reputation of being the bridge between ragtime and jazz. So, in the early days, I think you could call it ragtime. That's the name we heard. Well, about, do you have any information on Tom Brand, or could you give me the name of the gentleman that called about him? Because he seemed to be, you know what he was talking about. Yeah, his name is Eddie Chance. It might be spelled T-C-H-A-N-T-Z. Would you verify that? I believe that's right. Eddie Chance was his nephew. And Tom Brown played in my band, and Eddie Chance played in my band. And, of course, Eddie Chance can give you an awful lot of information about Tom Brown, and so can Dick Allen. Dick Allen has more information on jazz, I'm quite sure. I don't hesitate to say, than anybody in America.
